newsitem.title: JAPAN: 'Time bomb' starts ticking for dollar - traders.
newsitem.headline: 'Time bomb' starts ticking for dollar - traders.

text.p: The dollar may be on the verge of repeating its 1995 collapse against the yen, as U.S. patience with Japan's swelling trade surplus appears to be wearing thin, traders said on Wednesday.
"A time bomb, already set in April, has finally started ticking for the dollar," said a chief currency trader at a Japanese bank.

Takeshi Hanai, executive manager at the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd's International Treasury Department, added: "The dollar's downward spiral is unlikely to halt until the market experiences a 'dollar-selling peak' below 110 yen."

The dollar fell to a seven-month low of 110.97 yen on Wednesday after remarks by U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers that Japan should foster domestic demand-led recovery and avoid running up external surpluses.
The dollar has fallen a stunning 13 percent in just six weeks from a four-year-and-nine-month peak of 127.47 yen on May 1.

In April, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin clearly warned Japanese bureacrats during a visit to Tokyo that Washington would not wait indefinitely for Tokyo's peculiar policy mix to whittle down the country's trade surplus.

Tokyo has steadfastly held to a plan of fiscal restraint and sharp budget cuts, despite the dampening impact on domestic demand, while relying on aggressive economic deregulation to keep its economy moving forward and its surplus coming down.
But evidence has been mounting that, at least in the short-term, Japan's approach may not be working.
Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) on Wednesday said the surplus in Japan's current account rose 92.7 percent from a year earlier to 1.09 trillion yen ($9.8 billion) in April.

The downward pressure on the dollar sparked by rekindled Japan-U.S. trade tensions has been magnified by the greenback's heavily overbought position, which resulted largely from heavy Japanese investment in higher-yielding overseas assets, traders said.

"The dollar will surely take a dive below 100 yen as people who overbought dollars start to dump them in the market," said Toshihiko Masaki, a senior trader at the Long-term Credit Bank of Japan (LTCB).
The gap between U.S. and Japanese rates, gauged by benchmark bond yields, stood at 439 basis points on Wednesday, compared with a peak of 502.5 basis points in early April.
On Wednesday, MOF said that Japanese investors' foreign bond purchases hit a record high of 2.5783 trillion yen ($23.2 billion) in April, up sharply from 393 billion yen ($3.54 billion) in March.
"The (Japanese) monetary authorities are expected to intervene to try to brake the dollar's slide when it breaches 110 yen, but this time the dollar may not stop falling easily," said LTCB's Masaki.

In the two years to December 1996, Japan spent an estimated $64.73 billion on efforts to rein in the galloping yen, boosting Japan's external reserves to $221.761 billion, the highest in the world, by the end of May.
The Bank of Japan (BOJ) is expected to move aggressively to shore up the sagging dollar this time as well, traders said.
But, they added, the effectiveness of BOJ intervention in the near-term may be limited, as it would be greatly offset by the unwinding of long dollar positions by Japanese institutional investors.
